result: The authors generated CRISPR/Cas9 mutations in vsx1 (vsx1Δ245, an in-frame deletion of 53 amino acids) and vsx2 (vsx2Δ73, deleting 24 amino acids and generating a premature stop codon). Western blot analysis confirmed the absence of Vsx1 and Vsx2 proteins in vsxKO embryos at 24hpf, and no maternal Vsx1 protein was detected at 1.5hpf.
evaluation: Reviewers requested detailed characterization of the mutations including protein analysis. The revised manuscript provided western blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, d) demonstrating loss of protein, which Reviewer 2 acknowledged: 'provided protein analysis showing loss of vsx1/vsx2 protein in the mutants.' This addresses concerns about whether the alleles are true nulls.

result: Single homozygous mutants (vsx1Δ245 or vsx2Δ73) and animals with a single wild-type copy of either gene appeared normal and were fertile. Double mutant larvae (vsxKO) died at around 3 weeks post fertilization, with only one escaper reaching adulthood.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these viability observations. Reviewer 3 noted the lethality was 'not consistent with any other study on vsx mutants' and suggested exploring genetic background effects, but the data itself was accepted as reported.

result: Neural retina is properly specified and maintained in vsxKO embryos, which do not display microphthalmia. At 24hpf, optic cup morphology, size, proliferation rate, and RPE marker expression (tfec, bhlhe40) appeared normal. No trans-differentiation to pigmented cells was detected.
evaluation: This was initially a major concern. Reviewer 3 stated the 'lack of microphthalmia is an unexpected outcome' and requested early timepoint analysis. The authors added 24hpf data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing normal early specification. After revision, Reviewer 1 stated 'the evidence is now strong for the differences between the phenotypes generated by the Crispr mutants compared to the morpholinos,' indicating acceptance of this finding.

result: The onset of retinal differentiation appeared slightly delayed in vsxKO mutants as determined by atoh7 in situ hybridization at 26 hpf.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 requested analysis of neurogenesis markers at early timepoints. The authors provided atoh7 ISH data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h, i) showing a slight delay. This data was included in the revision and not challenged by reviewers.

result: Histological analysis revealed a small delay in IPL formation at 48hpf, disorganization of OPL and IPL at 72hpf, and at 6dpf, vsxKO larvae showed all retinal layers but with significantly increased ONL thickness and reduced INL thickness compared to wild-type.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these histological observations. The data is presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, with quantification. Reviewer 1 noted the study 'succeeds in revealing important distinctions in early vertebrate retinal development.'

result: vsxKO fish presented expanded pigmentation in skin melanocytes even when exposed to bright light, indicative of an impaired visual background adaptation (VBA) reflex associated with blindness.
evaluation: This phenotype is shown in Figure 1e, i and Figure 1—figure supplement 3. Reviewers did not challenge this observation, which is consistent with visual impairment documented by ERG and OKR assays.

result: ERG recordings showed that vsx2Δ73 response was similar to wild-type, while vsx1Δ245 showed reduced b-wave. In vsxKO double mutants, 26/36 larvae showed only a-wave with no b-wave, and 10/36 showed reduced b-wave. Statistical analysis confirmed significant b-wave reduction in vsx1 single and vsxKO double mutants. A single wild-type copy of vsx1 is sufficient to prevent ERG defects, indicating vsx2 loss can be compensated by vsx1.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'The data for visual impairment and reduced bipolar function is strong.' The ERG data (Figure 2) clearly demonstrates functional deficits. The compensation finding is well-supported by the genotype comparisons.

result: Optokinetic response (OKR) testing showed significantly reduced eye movement velocity in vsx1 single and vsxKO double mutants compared to vsx2Δ73 and wild-type controls across all conditions tested.
evaluation: This data is presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. Reviewers did not challenge these findings, which complement the ERG data in demonstrating visual impairment.

result: Proliferation analysis using PH3 staining showed no difference between wild-type and vsxKO at 24 and 48hpf. However, at 60hpf, vsxKO retinas showed significantly increased PH3+ cells, particularly in outer and peripheral regions. By 72hpf, proliferation returned to normal levels restricted to the CMZ.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 requested proliferation analysis at 24hpf and other early timepoints. The authors provided comprehensive PH3 data (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing the temporal dynamics. This data was not challenged in the second round of review.

result: Apoptosis analysis using cleaved caspase-3 (C3) staining showed rare C3+ cells at 60hpf in both wild-type and vsxKO. At 72 and 96hpf, vsxKO showed significantly increased apoptotic cells, concentrated mainly in the INL layer, with some C3+ cells also in the GCL.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 suggested that 'enhanced apoptosis in the INL at the 72 and 96 hpf timepoints could be indicating that bipolar fated precursors are dying.' The data (Figure 3h-n) clearly shows increased apoptosis in the INL. Reviewers did not challenge these findings after revision.

result: DiI/DiO tracing showed no obvious differences in retino-tectal projections between wild-type and vsxKO larvae at 6dpf, indicating that retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are not affected.
evaluation: This data is presented in Video 1. Reviewers did not challenge this finding. It helps establish that the visual defects are specifically related to bipolar cell dysfunction rather than RGC or projection defects.

result: Photoreceptor differentiation analysis showed mild downregulation of prdm1a at 72hpf and delayed differentiation of cones (Zpr1) and rods (Zpr3) at 72 and 96hpf. At 6dpf, Zpr1 fluorescent intensity was significantly increased in vsxKO, while rod staining showed no major differences, suggesting cone cells are overrepresented in the ONL.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 requested clarification of ONL thickness changes and photoreceptor populations. Reviewer 3 noted that 'The delay in photoreceptor gene expression was described here as a novel finding, but Rutherford et al. reported on a similar phenotype in the vsx2 mutant mouse.' The authors acknowledged this citation. The data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) supports delayed and altered photoreceptor differentiation.

result: Bipolar cell marker analysis showed normal prox1 expression at 48hpf, but altered nuclear distribution in the INL at 72hpf. The bipolar marker prkcbb was very reduced or absent in the INL at 72hpf in vsxKO, confirming that vsx genes are essential for bipolar cell specification in zebrafish.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'The data for visual impairment and reduced bipolar function is strong.' The marker data (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) combined with ERG and histology provides multiple lines of evidence for bipolar cell loss. This is a core finding of the paper.

result: Amacrine cell differentiation analysis using ptf1a and pax6 markers showed normal progression at 48 and 72hpf in vsxKO retinas, suggesting vsx genes do not play a major role in amacrine cell specification in zebrafish.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 noted 'The characterization of some cell types was rather cursory in detail' and that 'observations made for the ptf1a and prdm1a were not in agreement with the images shown.' The authors provided additional marker data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). After revision, this was not further challenged.

result: Müller glia marker analysis showed a clear increase in gfap expression in vsxKO retinas at 72hpf, suggesting Müller glia cells are overrepresented, potentially compensating for the reduction in bipolar cells.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted 'Another interesting observation from the study is the increase in MG cells based on GFAP staining' and discussed prior studies. The data (Figure 4d, h) clearly shows increased gfap. Reviewer 1 in the second round noted this finding and referenced Rowan et al. data on Müller glia in mouse mutants, accepting the observation.

result: Analysis of spinal cord interneurons showed no significant differences in V2a or V2b density between wild-type and vsxKO at 24hpf, suggesting V2 motoneurons are properly specified in vsxKO animals.
evaluation: This data is presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3. Reviewers did not challenge this finding, which helps establish the specificity of vsx function in the retina versus spinal cord in zebrafish.

result: ATAC-seq at 18hpf identified 1564 DNA regions with differential accessibility in vsxKO (633 more accessible, 571 less accessible with log2 fold change >|1.5|). Gene ontology analysis of 2219 genes neighboring these regions revealed terms related to neuronal differentiation and eye development, suggesting vsx mutation results in deregulation of hundreds of cis-regulatory elements associated with retinal genes.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 requested 'A table of the DOCR analysis from the ATAC seq should be provided, preferably the whole datasets' and 'Gene enrichment analyses (KEGG, GO, etc) should be done.' The authors provided this data (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1, 2). Reviewer 1 in round 2 requested clarification of datasets but did not challenge the findings themselves.

result: RNA-seq at 18hpf revealed expression changes in a relatively small gene set (1018 genes), with only 41 up-regulated and 31 down-regulated genes above log2 fold change >|1.5|. Only 3 up-regulated transcription factors (vsx1, znf1109, znf1102) and one down-regulated TF (znf1091) were above threshold. Among 2219 genes neighboring differentially open chromatin regions, only 5% (119) were associated with differentially expressed genes.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 requested 'A table of the differential gene expression analysis from the RNA-seq' and 'A table showing the 119 genes that are predicted to overlap by DEG and DOCR analysis.' The authors provided this data (Figure 5c, d; Figure 5—source data 3). The disconnect between chromatin changes and transcriptional changes is a key finding supporting the robustness interpretation.

result: qPCR analysis of core retinal GRN components at 19hpf showed significant expression changes only for rx2 and lhx2b (below threshold). vsx1 transcripts were significantly upregulated and vsx2 downregulated in vsxKO embryos. The general architecture of the retinal GRN was not significantly altered upon vsx mutation.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 noted 'Many of the genes analyzed are not necessarily retina specific and changes in expression could be obscured by the presence of other tissues.' The authors provided qPCR data (Figure 5e) and ISH confirmation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The minimal changes in core retinal genes support the robustness conclusion and were not challenged after revision.

result: Comparison of vsxKO mutants with vsx2 morphants by RNA-seq and PCA revealed very different regulatory responses. Core retinal network genes (rx3, rx1, six3b, vax2, lhx2b) appeared upregulated in morphants but not mutants. vsx2 expression was strongly downregulated in mutants but upregulated in morphants, suggesting the dysregulation induced by morpholinos is behind the early microphthalmia observed in morphants.
evaluation: This was a critical issue. Reviewer 3 stated 'the differences between prior morpholino data versus the mutant data here is troubling' and 'it is imperative to provide an explanation supported by data.' The authors generated new RNA-seq data comparing morphants and mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). Reviewer 2 in round 2 stated 'The morphant data helps solidify the differences in early phenotypes,' indicating acceptance of this explanation.

result: Analysis of medaka vsx1/vsx2.1 double mutants showed normal initial organ specification at 4dpf, but impaired INL differentiation and eye growth at later stages, with severe microphthalmia in larvae.
evaluation: This data is presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 3. Reviewers did not challenge these findings, which support the conclusion that vsx gene function varies across teleost species.

result: The authors conclude that genetic redundancy is an important mechanism sustaining the integrity of the retinal specification network, and that Vsx genes' regulatory weight varies substantially among vertebrate species. In zebrafish, Vsx genes do not play an early role in neural retina establishment, unlike in mice.
evaluation: This is the main conclusion of the paper. Initially, Reviewer 3 stated 'The main conclusion that the work provides insight into the robustness of the retinal specification network is not supported by data.' However, after extensive revision including morphant comparison, early timepoint analysis, and medaka data, the reviewers accepted this interpretation. The editor's summary states the study 'provides important insights into how tissue specification networks...can differ in their network architecture, resulting in differences in how they buffer perturbations.'

result: The authors conclude that Vsx genes have a conserved role in bipolar cell differentiation across vertebrates, with Vsx activity essential for bipolar cell differentiation in teleost fish, suggesting the genetic program was inherited from a common vertebrate ancestor.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'The data for visual impairment and reduced bipolar function is strong.' The bipolar cell phenotype is well-documented through multiple approaches (ERG, histology, markers). This conservation across species is not disputed by reviewers.

result: The authors show that retinal precursors unable to acquire bipolar fate follow alternative trajectories including apoptosis, extended proliferation, or differentiation as photoreceptors or Müller glia. The photoreceptor fate switch is consistent with mouse studies on Blimp1/Vsx2 antagonism. Delayed photoreceptor differentiation indicates Vsx activity is required for timing of differentiation.
evaluation: These interpretations are supported by the proliferation, apoptosis, and cell fate marker data. Reviewer 3 initially noted the photoreceptor delay was 'described here as a novel finding' but Rutherford et al. reported similar findings in mice. The authors acknowledged this. The overall interpretation of alternative cell fates was not challenged.

result: The authors argue that maternal rescue is unlikely because vsx transcripts are not detectable before zygotic genome activation, and that comparative transcriptomic analysis does not support genetic compensation acting as a relevant mechanism at optic cup stages.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raised concerns about 'maternal contributions of the wild type allele during early development.' The authors addressed this with western blot data showing no maternal Vsx1 protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) and citation to White et al. 2017 showing transcripts are not detectable before ZGA. The RNA-seq data showing minimal transcriptional changes argues against compensation. These explanations were accepted in revision.

result: The authors propose that gene redundancy within the retinal specification network, particularly among homeodomain transcription factors sharing the 5'-TAATT-3' motif (including vsx1, vsx2, rx1, rx2, rx3, lhx2b, lhx9, hmx1, hmx4), explains the absence of early phenotype in vsxKO embryos. Supporting evidence includes: other mutations in TFs targeting this motif don't compromise neural retina identity; even mouse vsx1/vsx2 double mutants retain differentiation potential; and mouse Vsx2 mutant defects can be partially restored by deleting a cell cycle gene.
evaluation: This mechanistic explanation is based on the authors' prior work (Buono et al. 2021) and literature synthesis. Reviewer 1 stated the study 'raises interesting questions about how the retinal GRN functions as a network in different species.' While reviewers note 'it still is not clear why this is happening,' they accept the redundancy explanation as the most parsimonious given the data. The editor's summary endorses this interpretation regarding 'yet-to-be-defined compensatory mechanisms.'
